name: David Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, David. I'm a field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you actually think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small firm, eight of us, that does energy retrofits on old terraced houses. So most days I'm on a scaffold fixing battens for external insulation, or inside lifting floorboards to stuff wool between the joists. I'm the junior, two years in, so I get the dusty jobs and I'm still learning to cut a clean mitre. Marek, who's Polish and the best carpenter I've worked with, is teaching me sash windows on Fridays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that every house we finish uses half the gas it did, and the old lady in it can afford to heat the back bedroom again. What wears me out is lugging insulation boards up three floors of scaffold in the rain, and how slow I still am on the finishing. I use AI every day, honestly, to price up materials for the boss, to translate when Marek's English runs out, and to watch how-to stuff on the bus home. My partner Theo jokes I talk to my phone more than to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that was a lot of fuss for a fancy search engine. Online I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly, because I was hoping it'd do more of the boring stuff. At work Marek would laugh at me for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, which is fine. The retrofit work is there for twenty years, there are millions of leaky houses. I'd just keep getting better and probably end up a proper carpenter by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Keep using the AI tools for pricing and learning, because they still help even if they don't change the world. Maybe I'd do a short course on heat pump installs next year, because that's where the work's going anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a film everyone hyped that turned out to be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. What were you hoping it would do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take the measuring and the cutting lists off us. I spend an hour at the end of each day typing up what boards we used, and it's dead time. I wanted AI that walks round the house with you and does the survey, so we can spend more time actually fixing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone at your firm feel differently about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, totally. He thinks if you can't do it with your hands and a pencil you don't really know it. He's probably right about the craft side, but he also spends twenty minutes adding up columns that my phone does in a second.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of fuss for a fancy search engine, and I'd admit online I was a bit disappointed. My colleague Marek would laugh at me for months.
S0.think: Privately nothing changes, which is fine, because retrofit work will be there for twenty years. He expects to become a proper carpenter by thirty.
S0.do: Keeps working on retrofits and using AI tools daily for pricing and learning. Considers a short heat pump installation course next year because that's where the work is heading.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, like an over-hyped film that turned out fine.
S0.quote: I wanted AI that walks round the house with you and does the survey, so we can spend more time actually fixing things.
S0.fieldNote: David is the rare junior who is disappointed when AI fizzles. He sees technology as a way to cut dead admin time, not as a threat. His confidence rests on the huge amount of retrofit work he believes is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, as long as the gains go to workers and not just the owners. Online I'd post about how retrofit needs millions of people and AI could make it faster and cheaper for the public. And I'd say government should fund training so it's not only the tech-savvy who keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the people who does all right. I already use the tools, I'm young, I like trying things. The bit that worries me is people like Marek, who are better than me at the actual job but won't touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the boss if I can be the one who trials whatever new kit we buy, like a scanning tool for surveys. I'd do the heat pump course this year rather than next. And I'd keep saving the bit I save, I've got about two months put by, which feels okay since I'd likely keep my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly excited. The only knot is for the older lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the boss said no to you trialling the new kit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably do it on the side anyway, try it on a mate's house for free and show him. That's how I got him to let me do the material orders with AI, I just did one and it came out cheaper. He's not against stuff, he just needs to see it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Marek worries you. What would you actually do for him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit with him and show him, but in a way that doesn't make him feel stupid. He taught me sash windows for nothing, so I'd teach him the scanner. It sounds soppy, but I think that's how it's meant to work in a small firm.

S1.say: I'd say steady change is a chance, as long as gains go to workers and not only owners. I'd post that government should fund training so everyone keeps up.
S1.think: Privately he expects to do well because he already uses the tools and likes trying things. He worries more about skilled older colleagues like Marek who won't touch it.
S1.do: Asks to trial any new kit such as a survey scanner and does a heat pump course this year. Keeps his two months of savings steady because he expects to keep his job.
S1.feel: Calm and mostly excited, with a knot of worry for older colleagues.
S1.quote: He taught me sash windows for nothing, so I'd teach him the scanner.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption feels like opportunity to David. His worry is outward, for a skilled mentor who resists tech, and he'd repay the teaching he got. He tends to prove new tools by doing rather than asking permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment we decide who owns the robots. If it's three companies, it's a disaster; if it's public or shared, it could be the best thing that ever happened. I'd be posting that and turning up to every meeting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me more than I'd admit online. Two years is too fast for anything fair to get set up, and I'd be twenty-nine with no school certificates and half a trade. Being good with AI tools doesn't help much when the AI doesn't need a person holding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. Keep in mind there are only about 2 years before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd learn everything I could about running and repairing the building robots, because someone has to install and fix them for a while. I'd push the boss to buy one early so our firm survives, and I'd get the eight of us talking about turning it into a co-op. I'd also save harder, aiming for four months, and join the union, which I've never bothered with because we're so small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm still doing things, but my stomach's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being good with AI doesn't help much here. That's a change from the earlier pictures.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is. In the slow one my skills are a head start. In this one, I'm a head start in a race that ends in two years, and then what? I'd still try, because doing nothing is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Theo talk about the first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. He's a teaching assistant, so we'd be wondering whether schools are next too. Then probably whether we should give up on saving for a flat and just keep the cash, because two months doesn't go far.

S2.say: I'd say this is the moment to decide who owns the robots: a few companies would be a disaster, public or shared ownership could be great. I'd post it and go to every meeting.
S2.think: Privately it scares him more than he'd admit: two years is too fast for anything fair, and he'd be twenty-nine with half a trade. Being good with AI doesn't help when AI doesn't need a person.
S2.do: Learns to run and repair building robots, pushes his boss to buy one early and suggests turning the firm into a co-op. Saves harder towards four months and joins a union for the first time.
S2.feel: Anxious, still acting but with a tight stomach.
S2.quote: In this one, I'm a head start in a race that ends in two years, and then what?
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture punctures his confidence: he notices himself that his skills only buy time. He responds by acting on several fronts at once, including ownership of the machines. There is a gap between his upbeat public framing and his private fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ownership right, if we start now. I'd push for co-ops and councils to own the building robots, so the savings go into more homes and lower bills, not shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits me quite well. I'd be in on the ground floor with the new machines, and still young. The hard part is I'd probably never become the carpenter Marek is, and part of me minds that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 5 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do a proper course on robotics for construction, evenings or day release if the boss allows. I'd push our firm to buy a robot in year two or three and offer to run it. And I'd join the union and the local housing campaign, because whoever has the robots in 2031 matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mostly hopeful way. I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose that you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Friday sash window lessons. There's something about Marek showing me how to fit a new pulley in a two-hundred-year-old frame. A robot might do it in the end, but nobody will teach anybody that anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you get the timing wrong, buying into a robot too early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Totally. The first machines might be rubbish and the firm could waste a lot of money. That's why I'd want to trial one on hire first, like we do with scaffold, before anyone buys anything.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ownership right if we start now. Co-ops and councils should own the building robots so savings go into homes, not shareholders.
S3.think: Privately five years suits him: he gets in early with the machines while still young. He minds that he'll probably never become the carpenter his mentor is.
S3.do: Takes a construction robotics course in year one and pushes his firm to hire then buy a robot in year two or three, offering to run it. Joins the union and a local housing campaign.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, because he can see a path.
S3.quote: A robot might do it in the end, but nobody will teach anybody that anymore.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, his adaptability becomes a plan. The real loss he names isn't income but the hand-to-hand teaching of an old craft. He's practical about risk, suggesting hiring before buying, like scaffold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be idiots to waste it. Shorter working weeks, public ownership of the big systems, and money for everyone to retrain, that's what I'd be posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels fine for me. I'd get a few good years as a carpenter, then move into whatever's new before it lands. By thirty-seven I'd want to be running the robots, or teaching people to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 10 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep at the carpentry and finish my trade certificate, because I never got school ones and I want something. Then the heat pump course, then maybe robotics around year three or four. I'd also get involved in politics locally, probably the housing campaign, because ten years is long enough to win a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. It feels like time to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry that ten years makes people too relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, people will treat it like climate change, always ten years away. My dad's like that. I'd be the annoying one at the pub going, no, it's actually coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change in your personal plans with Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep saving for a flat, probably, which we wouldn't in the fast one. Ten years is long enough that buying makes sense if I've got a plan. We might even get a dog.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift we'd be foolish to waste. I'd post about shorter weeks, public ownership of big systems and retraining money for everyone.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels fine: some good years as a carpenter, then a move into whatever is new. By thirty-seven he wants to be running robots or teaching others to.
S4.do: Finishes his trade certificate in the first year, then a heat pump course, then robotics around year three or four. Gets involved in his local housing campaign.
S4.feel: Calm and a little excited, with time to get it right.
S4.quote: I'd be the annoying one at the pub going, no, it's actually coming.
S4.fieldNote: The long horizon fits David's temperament: he plans a stepping-stone path and wants to be the one persuading others. He compares complacency about AGI to complacency about climate change. His personal plans, like buying a flat, survive in this picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because nothing fair gets built that fast. What would help is the robots being owned by councils or co-ops, not three giant companies, and a basic income while people work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the houses. There are millions of cold, leaky homes, and if robots can fix them cheaply, that's brilliant for people. I just want to be in the room when they decide who pays and who profits.

headlineQuote: Being good with AI tools doesn't help much when the AI doesn't need a person holding it.
portrait: David Baker is a 27-year-old junior on a small eco-retrofit firm, insulating old terraced houses and learning sash windows from his mentor Marek. He lives with his partner Theo, has about two months saved, and uses AI every day for pricing, translating and learning. He is calm, even a bit disappointed, if AI fizzles, and sees steady change as an opportunity. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious, because his tech skills only buy a short head start. With five or ten years he plans a path into running building robots and campaigns for councils or co-ops to own them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because nothing fair can be built that fast.
whatWouldHelp: Building robots owned by councils or co-ops rather than a few giant companies, and a basic income while people work out what's next.
